newsitem.title: UK: EMS/European holidays leave spotlight on punt.
newsitem.headline: EMS/European holidays leave spotlight on punt.

text.p: The mark was mixed on its European crosses in holiday-thinned trading, with the spotlight remaining on the Irish pound after its sharp slide Wednesday.
While most continental European centres were closed for the May 1 Labour Day holiday -- including Germany, France, Spain, Sweden, Belgium and Switzerland -- Irish markets were open.
Traders said the reasons behind the punt's slide yesterday remained in place and there was scope for further losses.
"The market has got the punt's ERM central rate in its sights now and it looks like this move has further to go," said Lee Ferridge, foreign exchange strategist at Commerzbank.

The punt fell as much as seven pfennigs, or more than three percent, on Wednesday amid speculation the Irish authorities are now keen to allow the currency to weaken toward its central rate in the European exchange rate mechanism at 2.4111 marks in preparation for European monetary union in 1999.

Crucially, the punt also fell sharply against sterling and is showing signs of decoupling from the UK unit which has been largely been responsible for dragging it more than 11 percent above its ERM parity this year.
At 0920 GMT, the punt was trading at 2.5758/73 marks compared with 2.5960/40 late Wednesday and 2.6675 on Monday.

Pressure on the punt began building after Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn said on April 15 that he was somewhat concerned with the punt's strength in the ERM and would prefer if it were closer to its ERM mid-point. Quinn helped stabilise the punt late Wednesday, however, when he said no decision had been made yet on EMU conversion rates.

Traders said central bank intervention to buoy the punt over the past couple of weeks was not sustainable and the Irish central bank was seen to withdraw from the market late Tuesday amid speculation about a sharp depletion of reserves. Irish offical reserves were about $8.6 billion in February.

Traders said a growing belief that conversion rates for currencies starting EMU will be at their central ERM rates prompted many foreign investors who were long of Irish government bonds and stocks to factor in the currency risk suddenly apparent in their Irish asset holdings.
"In many ways comments from the Bundesbank last Friday highlighted the issue to many people," said a trader at a major U.S. bank in London.
Bundesbank council member Peter Schmidhuber said in Dublin on Friday that the strength of the punt was a problem but should not prevent Ireland starting EMU.
Traders are now trying to work out how far the punt could retreat if the ERM central rate is seen to be the EMU conversion rate.

Some point out that the punt's return to notional 2.25 percent trading bands around 2.4111 will leave a target at the top of that band about 2.4650 marks. All other aspiring EMU members are currently trading within the pre-1993 2.25 percent ERM band around their ERM parities despite officially being allowed 15 percent fluctuation limits.
Others are looking to levels in the low 2.50's which would be consistent with a January 1999 forward rate of 2.4111.

If Ireland starts EMU and is fixed at its ERM central rate then the shrinkage of the interest rate gap with Germany to zero would mean that the spot rate must now trade at a premium to the conversion rate which allows for the implied depreciation shown in the forward market.
The policy risks of a trade-weighted slide in the punt are high, however, as it may exaggerate the already significant inflation risks associated with the booming Irish economy.
As a result, the market will be on the lookout for a rise in the Irish central bank's key interest rate, the 6.25 percent short-term facility (STF).
Elsewhere, the markets were gridlocked by a combination of the May Day holiday, Golden Week in Japan, the UK election and monthly market vigil ahead of the U.S. non-farm payrolls report, due Friday.
"In conditions like these, there are few people who will want to take any big market positions," said Ferridge at Commerzbank.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
